statement: Consider $x^{2}-2kx+2k^{2}-3=0$. (i) By completing the square as $(x-k)^{2}+(k^{2}-3)=0$, find the range of real $k$ for which the equation has real roots. (ii) Let the roots be $\alpha,\beta$. Show that $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is independent of $k$ and find its value. (iii) Show that whenever the roots are real, $|\alpha-\beta|\le 2\sqrt{3}$.
solution: (i) $(x-k)^{2}=3-k^{2}$, so real roots require $3-k^{2}\ge 0$, i.e. $|k|\le \sqrt{3}$. (ii) $\alpha+\beta=2k$, $\alpha\beta=2k^{2}-3$; thus $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(2k)^{2}-2(2k^{2}-3)=6$, independent of $k$. (iii) $(\alpha-\beta)^{2}=(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-4\alpha\beta=4k^{2}-4(2k^{2}-3)=12-4k^{2}\le 12$, so $|\alpha-\beta|\le \sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3}$.
hints: Complete the square to read off the condition.
Express alpha^2+beta^2 via the sum and product.
